mcqs.question: You want max-heap behavior from Python's heapq, which only implements a min-heap. What's the standard workaround?
options: Call heapq.heapify() with a reverse=True argument
Push and pop negated values, then negate the result again when reading it back out
Sort the underlying list in descending order after every push
Use a separate max_heapq module instead of heapq
mcqs.explanation: heapq has no reverse flag and no separate max-heap module, so the standard trick is negating values on the way in and back out: pushing -x makes the largest x the smallest -x, which heapq's min-heap naturally surfaces first. Sorting after every push would defeat the entire point of using a heap.

mcqs.question: Pushing tuples like (distance, node) into a min-heap is a common pattern for ordering by a custom key. Why does this work without writing an explicit comparator?
options: The heap ignores every field except the first one in a tuple
Tuples compare lexicographically by default, so ordering by the first element (with later elements only breaking ties) falls out for free
heapq automatically detects which tuple field is numeric and sorts by that
It only works if every element in the tuple is the same type
mcqs.explanation: Most languages compare tuples element by element left to right, so putting the priority key first makes tuple comparison do exactly what a custom comparator on that key would do — and it silently falls through to later elements only when the first elements are equal.

mcqs.question: You push (priority, task_object) tuples into a heap, and two tasks arrive with equal priority. task_object is a plain custom class with no comparison methods defined. What happens?
options: The heap silently drops one of the two tied entries
The tuple comparison falls through to comparing task_object directly, raising a runtime type error since it isn't orderable
The heap keeps both entries in arbitrary but valid order, no error occurs
Python automatically falls back to comparing the objects' memory addresses
mcqs.explanation: Tuple comparison only stops at the first field if it differs; on a tie it moves to the next field, and a custom object with no __lt__ defined raises a TypeError the moment that comparison is attempted. The standard fix is inserting an always-comparable tiebreaker (like an increasing counter) between the priority and the object.

mcqs.question: Dijkstra's algorithm is often described as needing a decrease-key operation. What's true about Python's heapq, Java's PriorityQueue, and C++'s std::priority_queue with respect to this?
options: None of the three built-ins support decrease-key at all — there is no method for it in any of them
All three support it via an update() or decreaseKey() method
Only C++'s std::priority_queue supports it, since it's a more advanced structure
It's supported but only for primitive numeric types, not custom objects
mcqs.explanation: None of the three mainstream built-in priority queues expose a decrease-key operation — finding an arbitrary element inside any of them is an O(n) scan since there's no index tracking positions. This is a standard-library limitation, not a fundamental one; specialized indexed heaps do support true decrease-key.

mcqs.question: Implementing Dijkstra's algorithm with a standard heapq-based queue, what's the practical workaround most implementations use instead of true decrease-key?
options: Rebuild the entire heap from scratch every time a shorter path is found
Push a new (shorter-distance, node) entry when a better path is found, and skip stale entries for an already-finalized node when popping
Switch to a linked list for the frontier instead of a heap
Use a separate hash map as the only priority structure, skipping the heap entirely
mcqs.explanation: Lazy deletion — pushing a fresh, better entry and ignoring outdated ones on pop — is what nearly every heapq-based Dijkstra actually does, since it needs no custom heap and is trivial to get right. It costs a little extra heap size for stale entries but avoids the complexity of a true indexed heap.

mcqs.question: You keep a reference to an object already pushed into a heap, and later mutate its priority field directly through that reference. What happens to the heap?
options: The heap automatically re-sifts the mutated object to its correct position
The mutation is rejected at runtime because the object is inside a heap
The heap's ordering invariant can silently become false for that object, since nothing knows to re-sift it — later pops may return elements in the wrong order with no error raised
Nothing changes because heaps store copies of pushed values, not references
mcqs.explanation: Heaps don't watch for external mutation and there's no automatic re-sift, so a direct mutation after push leaves stale, now-incorrect array positions with no exception raised — a silent correctness bug. The safe pattern is treating heap contents as immutable and using lazy deletion (push a fresh entry) if a priority needs to change.
